question: In recent days, the EEEKE1 announced that its members will serve up to 28 aircraft arrivals per hour at Athens International Airport, an increased number compared to the nominal capacity of 22, but not sufficient to meet air traffic demand, resulting in further delays.

The Greek Government and the competent services have been systematically indifferent to the long-standing problems in air traffic management, as despite the immediate need to modernise the systems and the three active infringement procedures against the country for noncompliance with European legislation,2 today, one and a half years after the Commission's reply3 to my previous question,4 no contract has been signed for the supply of new, modern air traffic control systems.

On the contrary, the entire burden is shifted to the extremely understaffed controller personnel, who are called upon to work with outdated technological equipment and communication systems and radars which are poorly maintained,5 without available spare parts, resulting in several cases of malfunctioning.6 In light of the above: 1.
What measures will the Commission take to ensure that Greece immediately acquires the necessary modern and reliable air traffic systems, in accordance with European requirements and legislation?

How will the Commission monitor whether there is adequate maintenance of the existing systems, as well as the availability of spare parts, so that these systems remain safe, reliable and operational until modern systems are purchased and activated?

answer: Greece is partially compliant with EU legislation on Air Traffic Management (ATM) (1) and there are three open infringement procedures regarding the deployment of datalink capabilities (2), the deployment of modern radars (3), and the publication of performance-based navigation (PBN) procedures at Greek airports (4).

On 11 December 2025, the Commission decided (5) to refer Greece to the Court of Justice of the European Union for failing to put in place the necessary measures to design and publish PBN procedures, and to send a reasoned opinion for failing to deploy modern radars.

The Hellenic Air Navigation Service Provider (HASP) is in charge of the adequate maintenance of the existing systems and the availability of spare parts. The Greek law 5240/2025 that has entered into force aims to grant to HASP the autonomy, resources, and capabilities to invest in staff and technology.

The Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority (H-CAA) is the national supervisory authority in charge of the daily oversight of HASP and is responsible for the enforcement of EU legislation on Air Traffic Management in Greece. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency supports the H-CAA by conducting regular standardisation visits and monitoring their safety oversight to assess compliance with EU regulations.
